newsitem.title: USA: U.S. must be leader in refugee care, report says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. must be leader in refugee care, report says.

text.p: A congressionally-appointed commission called on the White House on Friday to take charge of U.S immigration and refugee policies and criticised key measures of a new law, saying refugees could be wrongly returned to face persecution or death.

In its third report since 1994, the bi-partisan U.S. Commission on Immigration Reform said the White House National Security Council should take charge of overseeing all aspects of U.S. refugee policy, which are scattered among a number of agencies including the Immigration and Naturalisation Service.
It also called for "immediate correction" of measures in a law Congress passed last year that the commission said could wrongly return refugees to face persecution or death.
Refugee advocates said the report was a call for the United States to resume a leadership role in caring for the world's displaced and wronged.

"It is a ringing reaffirmation of the leadership role of the United States in immigration and refugee issues. Both the actions and the example of the United States are of enormous consequence in these issues," John Swenson, executive director of the U.S. Catholic Conference's immigration and refugee services, said.

"They are reaffirming a commitment to refugee admissions, and acknowledging that it's not so easy to determine who's a refugee anymore. With the end of the Cold War, ethnic tribal persecution is more what we're seeing and it's not so easy to pin down. It takes a lot of time and information and sensitivity," Jana Mason, congressional liason for the U.S. Commiittee for Refugees, said.

At a briefing, commission chairman Shirley Hufstedler said the law passed last year to curb illegal immigration had provisions "that we believe can harm bona fide asylum seekers and undermine the efficiency of the asylum system."

The law set a cap on annual grants of asylum to particular categories of refugees, required that people show a "credible fear" of persecution to continue their asylum application, and deported people if they committed offences that drew a prison sentence of a year or more.

Hufstedler said limiting grants of asylum could force the United States to violate its own laws and obligations by returning refugees to danger and persecution "merely because asylum numbers are unavailable," she said.

She said the "credible fear" standard could wrongly screen out people who were wary of authority or fearful of revealing wrongs done to them, and the prison rule could reject refugees for offences considered minor in this country.
The rule also made no distinction "between those who truly committed crimes and those jailed by a repressive regime on trumped-up charges to silence their opposition," she said.

The report also said the United States must become better at anticipating international and domestic refugee emergencies, and said it should negotiate "safe haven" agreements with other nations to provide asylum or temporary protection before there is a crisis.
